from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES', len(r.pages))
out = Path('tmp/pdfs'); out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with (out / 'manuscript.txt').open('w') as f:
    for i, p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
        t = p.extract_text()
        f.write(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n{t}\\n')
        print(f'PAGE {i}: {len(t)} characters')
print('\\nFIRST PAGE\\n', r.pages[0].extract_text())
PY"

strengths: WildFeedback addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring conversational feedback into preference supervision. The 20,281-pair dataset and model-specific variants offer a potentially useful resource for learning from multi-turn interactions.

Experiments cover three model families, three public benchmarks, and both expert-generated and on-policy preference pairs. Improvements over the original instruction-tuned models are substantial: Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3 to 34.9, and its Arena-Hard win rate from 15.4 to 32.4.

The authors regenerate UltraFeedback responses for stronger comparisons, explicitly separate training and test users/conversations, and conduct human audits of feedback detection and checklist evaluation. These are useful methodological safeguards.

The pipeline is generally clear. Appendices provide annotation rubrics, extraction and evaluation prompts, and key SFT/DPO hyperparameters. The limitations acknowledge selection bias and potentially harmful preferences.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users is only partially validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates preferred responses, filters on-policy pairs, and evaluates outputs. The human checklist audit reports 57.14% agreement and κ=0.372, versus human–human agreement of 63.27% and κ=0.436. This provides some validation, but no independent audit establishes checklist fidelity to original feedback, and no comparison shows that checklists improve agreement with humans. Figure 2 primarily demonstrates adherence to the generated checklists, rather than reduced evaluation bias.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational structure, response construction, and filtering. In the expert setting, WildFeedback also contrasts new GPT-4 responses with historical disliked responses, whereas UltraFeedback compares newly generated responses. Controls using the same WildChat prompts without feedback conditioning, alongside an SFT-only ablation, are needed to distinguish feedback benefits from distillation, domain adaptation, and preference-pair quality.

The 540-example test set deliberately selects common preferences within 70 clusters and tasks resembling training data. This fits the stated majority-preference objective, but does not establish representative coverage of real users. No randomly sampled comparison or minority-preference analysis is provided. Feedback detection also achieves only 48.4% DSAT recall, leaving substantial uncertainty about which feedback is excluded. Claims about diverse and evolving user preferences exceed the demonstrated scope.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a dataset-centered contribution. The manuscript only promises a future dataset release. Although training hyperparameters are supplied, generation decoding settings, clustering embeddings and similarity procedures, precise deduplication rules, and the validation criterion used for hyperparameter selection are insufficiently specified. Without the derived data and split artifacts, exact reconstruction would be difficult.

Claims of consistent and statistically significant superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. In Table 3, Qwen-2 trained on WF GPT-4 trails UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or training-seed variability are reported. The benchmark gains make Findings plausible, but the unresolved attribution, evaluation-validity, and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
